title: Roth IRA Calculator: how it works, formula and examples

content:
The [Roth IRA Calculator](/roth-ira-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Project tax-free Roth IRA growth — contributions, returns and years to retirement. Enter your current Roth IRA balance, your contribution per year, expected annual return and years until retirement and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Project what a Roth IRA could be worth at retirement. You contribute after-tax money — the 2025 limit is $7,000 under 50 or $8,000 at 50 and over — and qualified withdrawals in retirement are completely tax-free, including all the growth. That tax-free growth is the whole point of a Roth: the projection below shows how much of the final balance is your contributions and how much is growth you will never pay tax on.

## How to use the Roth IRA Calculator

Start by entering your current Roth IRA balance, then entering your your contribution per year, entering your expected annual return (%) and finally entering your years until retirement. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter your current Roth IRA balance.
2. Enter your yearly contribution — up to the $7,000 limit under 50.
3. Set the annual return you expect — 7% is a common planning figure.
4. Enter the years until retirement and read the projected balance and tax-free growth.

## Formula

Future value = balance × (1 + r)^n + yearly × ((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r, where r is the annual return and n the number of years. Growth = future value − balance − total contributions.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Roth IRA Calculator](/roth-ira-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. Starting with $5,000 and contributing $7,000 a year at a 7% annual return for 30 years, the projection is $699,286.78 — $210,000 of contributions plus $484,286.78 of growth, all of it tax-free on a qualified withdrawal. Try the same figures in the [Roth IRA Calculator](/roth-ira-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Current Roth IRA balance: 5000, Your contribution per year: 7000, Expected annual return: 7 %, Years until retirement: 30), the [Roth IRA Calculator](/roth-ira-calculator) returns Projected balance: $699,286.78, Total contributions: $210,000, Starting balance: $5,000, Tax-free growth: $484,286.78, 2025 contribution limit (under 50): $7,000. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Loan Calculator](/loan-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## The 2025 limits and income rules

For 2025 the Roth IRA contribution limit is $7,000 if you are under 50, or $8,000 at 50 and over. Unlike a 401(k), there is also an income limit: the ability to contribute directly phases out for higher earners (in 2025 the phase-out starts around $150,000 of modified adjusted gross income for single filers and $236,000 for married couples filing jointly). This calculator does not check your income — the limit line is a reminder to check whether you are eligible.

## Roth vs traditional IRA

A traditional IRA gives you a tax break now and taxes withdrawals later; a Roth takes the tax now and never taxes the money again. A Roth usually wins if you expect your tax rate in retirement to be the same or higher than today, and it has two extra perks: no required minimum distributions for the original owner, and your contributions (not the growth) can be withdrawn at any time without penalty.

## What this projection assumes

The calculation compounds once a year at a fixed rate with end-of-year contributions. Real returns vary, and the result assumes you contribute the full amount every year. It is an estimate for planning, not financial advice — for decisions about retirement accounts, speak to a qualified financial adviser.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Contribute early in the year if you can — the money gets up to twelve extra months of growth.
- If your income is above the Roth limit, ask a tax professional about a backdoor Roth IRA.
- Young earners in a low tax bracket usually get the most from a Roth, because the tax they pay now is small.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much can I contribute to a Roth IRA in 2025?

$7,000 if you are under 50, or $8,000 if you are 50 or older. There is also an income limit — the ability to contribute directly phases out for higher earners. Try it with your own numbers in the [Roth IRA Calculator](/roth-ira-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Are Roth IRA withdrawals really tax-free?

Qualified withdrawals are tax-free: the account must be open at least five years and you must be 59½ or older (with exceptions for disability or a first home). Your contributions can be withdrawn at any time without tax or penalty. Try it with your own numbers in the [Roth IRA Calculator](/roth-ira-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the difference between a Roth IRA and a 401(k)?

A 401(k) is through your employer with much higher limits ($23,500 for 2025) and often an employer match; a Roth IRA is an account you open yourself with a $7,000 limit but tax-free withdrawals. Many people use both. Try it with your own numbers in the [Roth IRA Calculator](/roth-ira-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Roth IRA Calculator use?

Future value = balance × (1 + r)^n + yearly × ((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r, where r is the annual return and n the number of years. Growth = future value − balance − total contributions.
